title: Anathapindika's last days
hookLine: dying, the great giver is taught not to cling to anything, and weeps at its depth

lines: THE ONE WHO FEEDS THE UNPROTECTED.
cards: Anathapindika's name, tradition says, means the one who gives food to the unprotected. He's the merchant who, in the tradition, bought Jeta's Grove for the Buddha by covering the ground with coins.

Again and again this year, a discourse has opened in the park he gave. Now he is very ill. He sends a man to pay his respects to the Buddha, and then to Sariputta with a request: please come, out of compassion.
Sariputta comes, with Ananda, and asks how he is. The answer is honest: the pain is getting worse, not better.

teach.h: PAIN LIKE A SWORD, A STRAP, COALS
teach.b: He describes it plainly, in the text's images: like a strong man splitting his head with a sharp sword, like a tight strap around the head, like a butcher's knife in the belly, like being held over hot coals.
Sariputta doesn't offer comfort first. He offers a training.

Train like this, householder: I won't cling to the eye, and my consciousness won't depend on the eye. Not to the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind. Not to sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches or thoughts.
Not to the elements, not to the five heaps. Not to this world, and my consciousness won't depend on this world. Not to any world beyond.
Not to anything seen, heard, sensed, known, sought or explored. Line after line, everything a dying person might hold. And Anathapindika weeps.
Ananda asks: are you sinking, householder? No, he says.

teach.h: HE WEEPS: I'VE NEVER HEARD THIS
teach.b: I've served the Teacher and the monks for so long, and I've never heard a talk like this.

teach.h: LET LAY PEOPLE HEAR IT TOO
teach.b: Sariputta answers that such talks are usually given to monastics, not to lay people. Before they go, Anathapindika asks for something.
Let talks like this be given to lay people too. There are those with little dust in their eyes who will be lost if they never hear it. Soon after they leave, he dies.
The text says he was reborn among the gods, and came back one night to Jeta's Grove, glowing, to praise it and Sariputta. The great giver's last gift was a request: share this with everyone.

how: Buddhist monks and friends visit the sick and the dying to chant and to recall teachings on non-clinging; MN 143 shows Sariputta doing exactly that.

o: a gift of land given to monks
a vow taken on one's deathbed

games.q: Anathapindika's last days: tap the pairs.
p: the one who feeds the unprotected
taught him not to cling to anything
lay people who'd benefit from hearing

s: Anathapindika weeps because he is afraid of dying
he says he has never heard such a deep talk in all his years of serving the Teacher.
he asks that talks like this be given to lay people too
some, he says, have little dust in their eyes and will be lost without hearing it.
the Buddha himself comes to the deathbed in MN 143
Anathapindika sends word to the Buddha, but Sariputta and Ananda are the ones who come.

games.q: you're Sariputta, at the bedside of a dying friend in great pain. what do you offer, in MN 143?
o: a training in not clinging to anything: senses, world, all of it.
a reminder of all his good deeds.
games.why: Sariputta teaches non-clinging, line by line, from the eye to every world. Anathapindika weeps at its depth.

practice: Choose one small thing you're holding today: a plan, an opinion, a worry about tomorrow, a feeling about yourself. Breathing in, notice how you hold it; breathing out, say quietly, in Sariputta's spirit: not clinging to this.
You don't have to throw it away, just loosen the grip for one breath, then another.

wordCard.voice: Upadana. Clinging, grasping: dying, the great giver Anathapindika hears Sariputta teach not clinging to anything at all, weeps at its depth, and asks that lay people hear it too. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali upadana: clinging, grasping. Sariputta teaches Anathapindika to let it go.

carryVoice: Your line: not clinging to this. A dying man's last request was that teachings like this reach lay people too. Go gently.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 143, Anathapindikovada Sutta (advice to Anathapindika)
